name: AnyList Complete
subcategory: family organization, recipes and household inventory
tagline: Manage shared grocery lists, recipes, and meal plans with a simple household sync server

tiers.limits: Household plan for the same Complete features shared by the household.

verdictSummary: The core loop is small enough for a capable coding agent to produce a useful local version in one sitting. For AnyList Complete, manage shared grocery lists, recipes, and meal plans with a simple household sync server. The hard boundary is excellent mobile capture, retailer integrations, voice assistants, and polished sharing, plus sync, integrations, and household adoption.
coreLoopDIY: Organize shared grocery lists, recipes, and meal plans on a simple household sync server, share or print a plan, and keep data portable and owner-controlled.
whatYouLose: excellent mobile capture, retailer integrations, voice assistants, and polished sharing
ongoingBurden: multi-user conflicts, reminders, notifications, imports, barcode data, smart-home APIs, backups, and long-term maintenance
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for AnyList Complete because household apps survive when every family member actually uses them and the data stays current across devices. The recurring cost buys multi-user conflicts, reminders, notifications, imports, barcode data, smart-home APIs, backups, and long-term maintenance, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Mealie
priorArt.desc: Active open-source recipe manager and meal planner for households.

alternatives.name: Grocy
alternatives.desc: Meal plans and groceries run through a tiny home ERP, because apparently the fridge needed one.

facts.install: Docker container/Compose, or install the PHP application on a web server
facts.dataFormat: Products, stock, chores, recipes, meal plans, shopping lists, and history live in Grocy's SQLite database inside its data directory; configuration, uploaded pictures, and generated files are stored alongside it on the host volume.
facts.gapVsPaid: Grocy is vastly more complex than a grocery list and lacks AnyList's fast native capture, voice-assistant integration, location-aware reminders, and polished household mobile sync.
facts.setupBlocker: The first obstacle is deploying and exposing a PHP/Docker web app; the larger practical hurdle is configuring locations, units, products, barcodes, and household routines before its ERP-like screens become useful.

alternatives.name: Mealie
alternatives.desc: A household recipe server with meal plans and grocery lists; you supply the server and patience.

facts.dataFormat: Recipes, users, groups, meal plans, and shopping-list records live in SQLite by default or PostgreSQL when configured; recipe images and application assets live in the mounted data directory, and Mealie's backup/export archives keep portable copies of the database and media.
facts.gapVsPaid: Mealie shares recipes and shopping lists, but its web-first recipe-server workflow is slower for aisle-side list entry, notifications, Siri/Alexa capture, and offline mobile use than AnyList.
facts.setupBlocker: A non-expert needs Docker, persistent volumes, an update/backup routine, and usually a domain plus HTTPS; importing recipe sites also produces parsing failures that must be cleaned up manually.

alternatives.name: RecipeSage
alternatives.desc: Shared recipes, meal plans, and shopping lists with no recipe cap; the polish budget is smaller.

facts.install: Hosted signup at RecipeSage, or Docker Compose for self-hosting
facts.dataFormat: The hosted service stores recipes, images, labels, meal plans, shopping lists, households, and account data in RecipeSage's infrastructure; self-hosting keeps the relational application database and uploaded media in operator-controlled containers/volumes, with built-in export for portability.
facts.gapVsPaid: RecipeSage covers shared recipes, plans, and lists, but its mobile polish, instant grocery entry, voice integration, offline behavior, and location reminders are weaker than AnyList's.
facts.setupBlocker: The public service has no setup blocker; self-hosting adds Docker, a database, mail, storage, HTTPS, and backups, while both versions have less refined native-mobile interaction than Paprika or AnyList.

alternatives.name: Samsung Food
alternatives.desc: Shared recipes, meal plans, and grocery lists for $0; Samsung gets the kitchen data instead.

facts.install: Install the mobile app or use the web app, then create a Samsung Food account
facts.dataFormat: Saved and imported recipes, meal plans, grocery lists, household-sharing records, profile data, and recommendations live in Samsung Food's cloud; the internal storage format is not disclosed.
facts.gapVsPaid: Samsung Food is free and polished, but ads and recommendation tracking replace AnyList's focused paid utility, and its grocery capture and voice/reminder workflow are less disciplined.

alternatives.name: Tandoor Recipes
alternatives.desc: The full recipe-plan-shopping loop; free for personal self-hosting, but the license is not actually open source.

facts.install: Docker Compose with PostgreSQL; manual Django deployment is also documented
facts.dataFormat: Recipes, users, meal plans, shopping lists, books, and permissions live in PostgreSQL in the standard Docker deployment; uploaded images and static/media files live in mounted volumes, and recipe data can be exported through Tandoor's export tools.
facts.gapVsPaid: Tandoor replaces a tiny household sync service with a Docker/PostgreSQL web app and lacks AnyList's frictionless native list entry, voice capture, reminders, and managed reliability.
facts.setupBlocker: The first obstacle is a multi-container Django/PostgreSQL deployment with secrets, volumes, HTTPS, email, and backups; its Commons-Clause-modified AGPL license is also not an OSI-approved open-source license.

rejectedAlternatives.name: AnyList Free
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Shared grocery lists are free; recipes and meal planning are exactly what Complete sells.

rejectedAlternatives.name: KitchenOwl
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Polished enough to tempt you; the project still labels itself Public Alpha.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Complete plan and a single-household organizer DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for AnyList Complete in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, SQLite, Drizzle ORM, and a local-first PWA; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: organize shared grocery lists, recipes, and meal plans on a simple household sync server, share or print a plan, and keep data portable and owner-controlled.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create household members, shared lists, calendar items, recipes or inventory records, and assignments.
Provide fast mobile-first capture with large controls, offline queueing, and conflict-safe sync to one server.
Support recurring chores or events, reminders, completion history, and printable views.
Add CSV or JSON import and export plus photo attachments with clear size limits.
Allow private and shared items and make every change attributable and undoable.
Add backups, household export, member removal, and a simple invite code.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out retailer ordering and proprietary product catalogs.
Deliberately leave out broad smart-home integrations.
Deliberately leave out large public recipe libraries and polished native mobile clients.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
